messages.subject: Planning bird surveys
parts:
Dear all, I am planning a bird abundance estimation survey and want to read something about the number of transects or points I should do and its relation with site area.

Thank you very much for any suggestion. 

Best wishes,
Joaquín

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Planning bird surveys
parts:
Joaquin

Welcome to the list.  There is an abundance of information online that can assist in your organising of your survey.  The most important element is for you to conduct a pilot survey; a small survey to give an idea of the number of bird detections you are likely to encounter per unit of effort (are you intending to walk transects, or conduct the survey using point transects?).  With results of the pilot survey and an idea of the precision you wish to achieve with your survey (coefficient of variation), you can apply some simple formulas to arrive an an approximation for the number of points or length of lines you would need to achieve the desired precision.  Note, this has little to do with the actual size of the study area.

To begin, I suggest you have a look at our online workshop materials:
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/
In particular, Chapter 4 has lectures dealing with survey design, and specifically determination of adequate sample size:
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter4/#determination-of-adequate-sample-size
In addition, I would recommend reading of Buckland (2006):

Buckland, S. T. 2006. Point transect surveys for songbirds: robust methodologies. The Auk 123 (2): 345–345. https://doi.org/10.1642/0004-8038(2006)123[345:psfsrm]2.0.co;2.

After looking at these materials, let us know if you have further questions.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Planning bird surveys
parts:
Thank you very much Eric! very valuable information! I´m working on it. I have previous data and recorded 60 observations of my species along 5 km total length (five transects of 1 km each). According to the formula L should be 22 km, which means 22 transects of 1 km  each for a 10% CV (1 km is an adequate length because of paddock sizes). And n=300, so I need to observe at least 300 birds or clusters in my study area. Does it make sense?
Best wishes, 
Joaquín

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Planning bird surveys
parts:
Joaquin

Using the formula for sample size with line transects based upon your pilot study information, I get a slightly different result:

Estimated amount of effort:

(3/(0.1^2)) * (5/60) = 25

25 * (60/5) = 300

Recognise that this formula is used to estimate the amount of effort necessary to estimate encounter rate accurately.  The total number of detections resulting from that amount of effort (300 in your case) is of secondary interest.

The assumption is that the region over which you conducted your pilot study is representative of the area over which you are performing the actual survey.  Of course, if during your pilot study, you only visited high density regions, your estimates of effort would not be representative of the entire study area.

El mar., 4 feb. 2020 a las 5:10, Eric Rexstad (<er...@st-andrews.ac.uk>) escribió:
Joaquin

Using the formula for sample size with line transects based upon your pilot study information, I get a slightly different result:

Estimated amount of effort:

(3/(0.1^2)) * (5/60) = 25

25 * (60/5) = 300

Recognise that this formula is used to estimate the amount of effort necessary to estimate encounter rate accurately.  The total number of detections resulting from that amount of effort (300 in your case) is of secondary interest.

El lun., 3 feb. 2020 a las 13:30, Eric Rexstad (<er...@st-andrews.ac.uk>) escribió:
Joaquin

Welcome to the list.  There is an abundance of information online that can assist in your organising of your survey.  The most important element is for you to conduct a pilot survey; a small survey to give an idea of the number of bird detections you are likely to encounter per unit of effort (are you intending to walk transects, or conduct the survey using point transects?).  With results of the pilot survey and an idea of the precision you wish to achieve with your survey (coefficient of variation), you can apply some simple formulas to arrive an an approximation for the number of points or length of lines you would need to achieve the desired precision.  Note, this has little to do with the actual size of the study area.

To begin, I suggest you have a look at our online workshop materials:
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/
In particular, Chapter 4 has lectures dealing with survey design, and specifically determination of adequate sample size:
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter4/#determination-of-adequate-sample-size
In addition, I would recommend reading of Buckland (2006):

Buckland, S. T. 2006. Point transect surveys for songbirds: robust methodologies. The Auk 123 (2): 345–345. https://doi.org/10.1642/0004-8038(2006)123[345:psfsrm]2.0.co;2.

After looking at these materials, let us know if you have further questions.
